newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Triumphant rebel leader sweeps into Zaire's second city.
newsitem.headline: Triumphant rebel leader sweeps into Zaire's second city.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila arrived in Lubumubashi on Monday to a tumultuous welcome from the people of Zaire's second city, taken over by his forces four days ago.

Kabila flew from his Goma headquarters in eastern Zaire to Lubumbashi airport, where troops of Zaire President Mobutu Sese Seko's presidential guard had attempted to resist his capture of the city last week.
He rode into town in a green Mercedes jeep in the middle of a column of pickup trucks loaded with his soldiers.

Heavily-armed troops were stationed every 100 metres in the tall grass lining the road from the airport. Church bells rang out and jubilant crowds waved branches, whistled piercingly and shouted Kabila's name.
The capital of mineral-rich Shaba province, a city of over one million in a state with a history of separatist revolt, is Kabila's biggest prize to date but perhaps his trickiest political challenge.
Some factions on Monday accused him of trampling on their political rights by appointing an interim governor here instead of holding immediate elections.

Kabila was expected to hold a victory rally in Lubumubashi, formerly the Belgian Congo town of Elisabethville, which expands his effective control to over half of Zaire, a country the size of Western Europe.

On Sunday, ministers from his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) flew into the city and announced over local television that Gaetan Kakudji would act as interim governor of Shaba.

"It's a coup d'etat. It's one dictatorship replacing another," said the spokesman for an angry group of supporters of Kyungu wa Kumwanza, the incumbent governor who they said had prepared the way for the rebels' takeover of the city by urging the Zaire army not to fight.

An AFDL spokesman, who declined to elaborate, said "confusion" among the people precluded an instant election of local administrators such as the Alliance had carried out in regions taken earlier in the six-month revolt to topple the regime of President Mobutu Sese Seko.

Earlier, Kabila's Finance Minister Mwana Nanga Mawampanga said the big foreign companies which help Zaire to mine its rich deposits of copper, cobalt, diamonds and gold could continue for the time being "within the framework of their present arrangements".
"A bad contract is better than no contract at all," he explained. But in time, "we are going to look at the fine print and make sure that we improve those contracts that can be improved".

The Alliance says it intends to establish a "social market economy" which will be attractive to investors but will also ensure a share of mineral-generated wealth to poor Zaireans who have been robbed of their heritage under Mobutu.
The finance minister said the worldwide diamond cartel De Beers had been told it would not be permitted to continue holding a monopoly on diamond buying in Zaire.

"They are based on monopoly and we don't want any more monopolies in this country. There must be competition. We will not tolerate monopolistic behaviour," Mawampanga said. "Everyone must play by the rules. The world has changed," he added.
